title: Security review - BYO/HSM provisioning workflow with AeroOrbit Satcom
summary: High-level walkthrough of Redwood's BYOK/HSM onboarding and multi-tenant provisioning patterns. Discussed options for customer-managed keys, HSM import vs remote wrapping, attestation requirements, audit logging, regional residency, and operational runbooks. Customer requested detailed runbook, FIPS attestation, and an architecture diagram showing key flow for satellite-ground processing. Agreed to schedule a hands-on technical deep dive and to run a short POC for import/unwrap latency tests.
topics: Audit logs and key access trails
Data residency and cross-border key transit
action_items: Alex Reed | Share BYOK runbook (PDF) and diagram showing key flow through Redwood runtime | 2026-10-12
Maya Chen | Prepare HSM attestation summary and FIPS validation links, include our HSM vendor contact | 2026-10-14
Marco Silva | Provide sample key sizes and expected QPS for telemetry decryption to size HSM pool | 2026-10-13
Priya Nair | Confirm internal policy on cross-border key material movement and list allowed regions | 2026-10-15
next_steps: Schedule hands-on technical deep dive (HSM import live demo) week of 2026-10-18
Run a 48-hour POC for unwrap latency with 1k requests/min from EU region
Send SOC 2 + ISO evidence links and current audit window dates
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-08
Time: 15:00 PDT / 23:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Ethan (CTO - AeroOrbit), Priya (Head of Security), Marco (Infra), Leila (Compliance)

[00:00] Alex Reed: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we scheduled a deep security and BYOK run today, quick intro from our side, i'm alex reed, i'm the account owner, maya here is our systems engineer who will lead the H-S-M specifics, maya you want to intro?
[00:12] Maya Chen: yeah hi all, maya chen, SE focused on crypto and infra, i've been through several BYOK and HSM onboards, we typically cover import, unwrap latency, attestation, and ops runbooks, i'll take the deep bits.
[00:25] Ethan Cole: great thanks, just to set context we are aeroorbit satcom, we process telemetry and some PII-ish metadata from ground stations, our ask is we need customer-managed keys in a way that's auditable and keeps certain keys inside EU and US only, and we need proof for our auditors — soc two and iso 27001.
[00:45] Priya Nair: and side note we have a policy forbidding plaintext key transit over public internet, except via approved secure enclaves or wrapped import mechanisms.
[00:54] Alex Reed: yep that's exactly what we'll cover. quick agenda, 1) explain our BYOK patterns — import vs remote wrap, 2) H-S-M attestation / FIPS posture, 3) multi-tenant provisioning model, 4) audit logging and RBAC for key ops, then q's and next steps.
[01:10] Marco Silva: quick question on terminology, when you say import, do you mean we generate keys in our HSM and then upload them to Redwood's H-S-M or do you mean we hand you wrapped blobs? we prefer not to send unwrapped key material.
[01:25] Maya Chen: good question — we support two patterns: customer-imported key material (you generate locally and we accept a wrapped import token) and customer-managed external KMS where we call your KMS via remote-unwrap or we perform an envelope wrap where the key never leaves your HSM unwrapped. in practice the flow is: you generate key -> wrap with import-wrapping key -> send wrapped blob to us -> we import into our HSM under customer tenancy.
[01:50] Leila Ortiz: is that compatible with our control requirement for split-knowledge during provisioning? auditors want confirmation that no single operator at redwood can reconstruct the key.
[02:02] Maya Chen: yes we have split-knowledge import options and require dual-operator confirmation for initial import when requested. sometimes customers prefer an offline handoff where the import token is transferred through a secure courier, but usually wrapped import and HSM key ceremony works.
[02:18] Ethan Cole: ok, can you speak to attestation — our external auditor asked about remote attestation evidence, we need to show we ran a vendor attestation and that the hardware is FIPS 140-2 level 3 or 140-3 equivalent.
[02:33] Maya Chen: our current HSM vendor has FIPS 140-2 L3 and they're in the process of 140-3 validation, we can provide the certs and the vendor attestation letters. we also produce HSM audit logs and a tamper-evident export trail — i'll attach those.
[02:48] Priya Nair: does redwood hold the import-wrapping key, or is that generated per-customer? we need guarantees that our wrapping key isn't co-used.
[02:58] Alex Reed: wrapping keys are per-customer and can be customer-controlled. for most BYOK flows the import wrapping key is derived in your HSM, you wrap locally, we only receive the wrapped blob. we do keep a record of the import operation in the audit logs but not the unwrapped material.
[03:15] Marco Silva: what's the latency implication? our pipeline decrypts telemetry at ingestion, so we need sub-20ms unwrap times ideally — can HSM imports or calls introduce a steady-state latency?
[03:27] Maya Chen: there are two considerations: import is a one-time operation and doesn't affect runtime. unwraps for envelope encryption at runtime depend on whether you want per-request unwrap (bad perf) vs using a per-process data key cached in KV cache. our model is: unwrap once, store data key in encrypted KV (or use a KEK in HSM for wrapping) and then use local symmetric ops for per-message decrypts. typical pattern yields <5ms per-decrypt after caching, initial unwrap could be 30-80ms depending on region and H-S-M.
[03:58] Ethan Cole: 30-80ms for initial unwrap is ok, we mainly care about throughput when many nodes start at once or during failover. do you support pre-warming or batch unwrap?
[04:10] Maya Chen: yes we support pre-warm jobs, and we can provision a warmed pool on startup to do parallel unwraps. for failover we suggest staggered rotation with leader elections to avoid thundering herd.
[04:25] Leila Ortiz: about audit logs — do you provide immutable audit trails for key usage? auditors want an append-only trail with exportable proofs.
[04:34] Alex Reed: we capture key lifecycle events: import, rotate, export attempt, access by service identity, operator actions. logs are write-once in our internal log store and we produce digest snapshots you can fetch. for enterprise customers we can ship syslog/S3 exports to your audit storage as well.
[04:52] Priya Nair: how long do you retain operator-level logs by default? and can retention be configured per-tenant for compliance?
[05:00] Maya Chen: default retention is 90 days in the console, but enterprise plans allow custom retention policy and long term export to your S3 for 7+ years if needed.
[05:10] Ethan Cole: data residency question — some keys must never leave EU, others can be global. can we map keys to regions and ensure routing?
[05:20] Alex Reed: yes, routing policies can pin keys to specific regional HSMs. our control plane supports region-scoped key stores and smart routing so requests for EU-pinned keys are handled in EU-only infra; we also provide automatic fallback to compatible region only if explicitly allowed.
[05:36] Marco Silva: what about cross-border backups and escrow? if we want offline escrow for disaster recovery, can the escrowed material be stored in a specific vault region?
[05:46] Maya Chen: escrow/backup can be configured per-key and per-region. we support encrypted escrows that you hold the split-escrow shares for, and we can keep the other shares in a region you specify. export/escrow operations require multi-party approval.
[06:01] Ethan Cole: can you describe the operator RBAC model? we have tiered operator roles in our SOC docs.
[06:09] Alex Reed: we implement RBAC with role definitions mapped to SSO assertions (SAML/OIDC). roles include key-admin (can import/rotate), key-ops (can request usage), auditor (read-only audit logs), and emergency-ops (break-glass with justification). every operator action is tied to SSO identity and 2FA can be enforced via your IdP.
[06:28] Priya Nair: do you support attribute-based access control for finer-grain rules, like only allowing certain IP ranges or only during maintenance windows?
[06:36] Maya Chen: yes we have policies that use attributes from the SAML assertion plus network context. we can enforce allow-lists and maintenance windows as part of the policy engine.
[06:44] Marco Silva: curious about key rotation — can Redwood perform automatic rotation with customer-supplied rotation windows, and can we opt for zero-downtime rotation where both old and new keys are accepted?
[06:56] Maya Chen: automated rotation is supported. the rotation is usually an orchestrated rollover: generate new key, re-wrap data keys or re-encrypt blobs, then retire old key after confirmation. zero-downtime patterns are supported with overlapping acceptance windows and lazy re-encryption.
[07:12] Ethan Cole: auditors will ask about proof that rotate operations happened — does the log show before/after key fingerprints?
[07:20] Alex Reed: yes, the audit entry contains key IDs, thumbprints, actor identity, and the operation reason. we also timestamp and include hash digests of the key material metadata (not the key itself).
[07:32] Leila Ortiz: one more — HSM firmware updates and tamper events, can we get notifications?
[07:40] Maya Chen: we publish HSM maintenance windows and firmware CVE advisories; tamper events trigger immediate alerts and we provide forensic bundles for customers with the enterprise tier.
[07:52] Ethan Cole: excellent. a couple of hypothetical flows — 1) we want to host KMS ourself and just have Redwood call our KMS for unwrapping, 2) we want fully BYOK so Redwood holds imported wrapped keys but with split-knowledge. pros/cons?
[08:08] Maya Chen: calling your KMS (remote unwrap) means you keep full key custody and we never hold key material, which is ideal for maximum control but adds network dependency and can add latency. imported BYOK (wrapped import) gives better runtime latency because keys live in our HSM, but custody is shared in the sense that an imported key lives in our infrastructure — we mitigate with per-customer HSM partitions, split-knowledge ceremonies, and strict RBAC and attestation. decision depends on whether you prioritize control or latency.
[08:39] Marco Silva: if we go imported BYOK, what's the process for rekeying a compromised key? we need a plan for key revocation and re-encrypting existing telemetry blobs without data loss.
[08:50] Maya Chen: we support revocation and rekey ops: you mark key compromised, issue a rotation job which generates a replacement KEK and rewraps data keys. we can do rolling re-encrypts or on-access lazy re-encryption depending on data volume. we'll help size the job and propose a schedule.
[09:05] Priya Nair: on evidence for auditors, can you provide your SOC 2 report and ISO certs and also a write-up of the BYOK controls?
[09:14] Alex Reed: yes we'll send the SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs and a BYOK control whitepaper.
[09:20] Ethan Cole: let's talk about tokenization of key import — do you have a hardware token or import token flow that we can use for air-gapped generation?
[09:29] Maya Chen: we support an offline import token flow: you generate key in air-gapped HSM, create import-wrapping envelope, transfer wrapped blob via secure medium to us. we also support hardware security modules that can do a secure transfer with split-escrow. some customers prefer courier-based key transfer for highest assurance.
[09:47] Marco Silva: operationally, where do we configure these per-key policies? in the console or via API? we want IaC integration.
[09:54] Alex Reed: both — console for visualization and API/SDK (Terraform provider) for IaC. the API supports key policy objects that you can version alongside infra code.
[10:05] Leila Ortiz: do you support attestable key provenance that we can snapshot and include in audit packages?
[10:12] Maya Chen: yes we can produce provenance bundles with key metadata, PKCS#7 signed digests, and import ceremony logs. those are useful in audits.
[10:22] Ethan Cole: network controls — do you allow customers to restrict which Redwood-hosted services can request key operations, e.g., only a named ingestion microservice?
[10:31] Maya Chen: yes service identities are part of the RBAC model; you can grant key usage only to specific service principals and require mTLS between service and Redwood runtime.
[10:40] Marco Silva: about HSM-backed TLS for ground station-facing endpoints, can Redwood terminate TLS with keys in HSM or must it be at app layer?
[10:49] Maya Chen: we can provision cert private keys in HSM for TLS termination at the gateway layer, yes. private keys can be stored in HSM and used by our edge termination proxies.
[10:58] Ethan Cole: interesting. any limits on key types/algorithms? we use EC P-256 and some legacy RSA 2048 for interop.
[11:06] Maya Chen: we support common RSA and EC curves (P-256, P-384) and some post-quantum hybrids on request; legacy RSA 2048 supported but we recommend migrating to EC.
[11:16] Alex Reed: quick poll — is the team leaning toward remote unwrap (you keep full custody) or wrapped import (latency benefit)?
[11:22] Priya Nair: by policy we prefer to keep custody where possible, but we may accept imported keys for telemetry that has stricter latency needs, provided we get strong attestation and escrow controls.
[11:34] Ethan Cole: same. maybe hybrid — keep master KEKs in our KMS for most sensitive data, import lower-sensitivity telemetry keys for performance.
[11:44] Maya Chen: that's a common hybrid approach — master K E K in your KMS, per-tenant data keys imported or generated in our HSM and wrapped by the KEK as needed.
[11:56] Marco Silva: question about liability and access during e-discovery or legal holds — if law enforcement requests access, do you have a process and will you notify us? what's your policy?
[12:06] Alex Reed: we follow legal process and will notify customers unless prohibited by law. we can include notification clauses in contracts. we also maintain transparency logs for legal access requests in enterprise contracts.
[12:18] Leila Ortiz: circling back to key rotation windows — auditors sometimes require rotation every 90 days for certain keys; can you automate that and produce proof?
[12:27] Maya Chen: yes rotation schedules are policy-driven and we can emit rotation attestations and logs showing the actual rotation timestamps.
[12:35] Ethan Cole: any SLA implications for keys pinned to a single region vs globally routed?
[12:42] Alex Reed: region-pinned keys have regional redundancy but if a region goes down and you disallow fallback, that could affect availability — SLA terms can reflect accepted fallback policies, and we can provide regional SLA variants.
[12:57] Marco Silva: about encryption at rest and in transit best practices, any Redwood-specific suggestions for our ingestion pipeline?
[13:04] Maya Chen: encrypt data at rest with envelope encryption (data keys wrapped by KEKs in HSM). for in-transit use mTLS with client certs backed by HSM keys and rotate certs with short TTLs. also use truncated logging to avoid sensitive payloads.
[13:22] Ethan Cole: good. can you walk briefly through the actual import ceremony steps so I can document in our audit package?
[13:29] Maya Chen: sure — step 1: customer generates KEK in their HSM and exports a wrapped import envelope, step 2: customer uploads blob via secure API or physical device, step 3: Redwood validates blob integrity, performs multi-operator approval if requested, step 4: Redwood imports wrapped key into tenant HSM partition, step 5: system records import event in immutable audit log and issues a signed provenance bundle. optional: escrow shares created and distributed.
[13:55] Priya Nair: and who signs the provenance bundle?
[13:59] Maya Chen: our HSM signs the metadata and an operator signs the approval step; we produce a PKCS7 signed bundle.
[14:06] Ethan Cole: good. about offline backups — do you support export of encrypted key backups that we can keep in our vault?
[14:14] Maya Chen: yes, encrypted export is supported and we can encrypt the export with a customer-public key so only you can decrypt.
[14:21] Marco Silva: detection and alerting — if there is an unexpected key access, can we integrate that into our pager duty?
[14:27] Alex Reed: yes alerts can flow to your SIEM/PagerDuty, and we can escalate high-severity events automatically.
[14:34] Ethan Cole: what about supply chain — do you allow customers to use a specific HSM vendor or only the vendor Redwood uses?
[14:42] Maya Chen: by default we standardize on a vendor for scale, but enterprise customers can request specific HSM vendors (subject to compatibility and validation). some customers run Redwood private with their chosen HSM in their VPC.
[14:54] Priya Nair: that last bit is important — we'd prefer Redwood Private with our HSM in our VPC if possible. is that an option?
[15:01] Alex Reed: yes Redwood Private supports customer-provided HSMs in VPC or on-prem, we offer an on-prem package and private control plane. we'll scope connectivity and support.
[15:09] Ethan Cole: perfect. any blockers around egress / ingress for satellite data when keys live in different regions?
[15:18] Maya Chen: main consideration is latency and compliance — if telemetry crosses borders but keys are pinned, you need to route decryption to the region or use local caching of data keys after secure unwrap. network egress rules can be configured to ensure decrypted payloads don't leave allowed regions.
[15:31] Marco Silva: what about cryptographic agility — post-quantum readiness?
[15:36] Maya Chen: we have PQ hybrid options and can support migrations; for now we recommend hybrid modes for the long-lived keys and we can run an eval.
[15:44] Alex Reed: want to open it up for any remaining questions?
[15:47] Priya Nair: yes, one more — penetration testing and vulnerability disclosure, do you allow us to run pen tests that exercise key operations?
[15:56] Maya Chen: yes under our pentest policy and with a coordinated window; key operations tests require extra controls so we can co-run to avoid accidental key compromise.
[16:06] Ethan Cole: excellent. we're sounding close to action items. any concerns from redwood side about hybrid approach?
[16:12] Alex Reed: none operationally — hybrid is normal. we'll provide diagrams and run the POC.
[16:18] Marco Silva: okay let's confirm timelines and owners — we need the runbook and attestation materials.
[16:24] Alex Reed: noted, and we'll set up the HSM import demo for the week of Oct 18.
[16:29] Leila Ortiz: auditors will want the BYOK control narrative — please include that in the runbook.
[16:34] Maya Chen: will do.
[16:36] Ethan Cole: any final closing notes?
[16:39] Alex Reed: we'll follow up in email with the docs and Doodle for the demo slot, thanks everyone.
[16:46] Meeting end notes: the transcript ends here. We had some cross talk and a couple of audio drops around 00:58 and 10:05 where the system labeled sprays of words incoherently (noted in the raw audio). The group is primarily oriented to a BYOK-hybrid solution and asked for runbook + attestation + POC for unwrap latency.
